current_episode.title: 131. Brooklyn Real Estate: Development, Distress & Opportunity in 2026 featuring Sean R. Kelly, Esq.

guest.bio_context: Sean Kelly has been in the commercial real estate business for almost 20 years, focusing heavily on development deals and the Brooklyn market. He works alongside Shimon Shkuri at Ariel Property Advisors, where he specializes in analyzing market trends, zoning initiatives, and investment opportunities in rent-stabilized and development sectors across Brooklyn.

context.real_quote: We've experienced significant change in the rent stabilization housing stock since the passage of HSTPA, and this is the first time in my career—almost 20 years—that we're seeing long owners, patient capital, family offices exit.
key_stats: $3.5 billion in Brooklyn commercial real estate transactions in the first six months of 2026, 15% higher than the prior year
$1 billion in development transactions in the first half of 2026, representing a 60% year-over-year increase
$300 million of the $1 billion development transactions from the greater downtown Brooklyn area
700 units created by the Navy Yard rezoning project in Clinton Hill post-COVID
$130 million in completed affordable housing and development sales in Brooklyn year-to-date, with another $100 million in contract
$30+ million rent-stabilized portfolio sold by Lethrax
0% rent increase orders affecting rent-stabilized property owners
entities: HSTPA (Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act)

This program is brought to you by Ariel Property Advisors. Hi everybody, this is Shimon Shkuri with Ariel Property Advisors and here with our Coffee and Cap Rates podcast. And today I have a very special guest. His name is Sean Kelly and he's my partner at Ariel Property Advisors. focuses a lot on Brooklyn. Don, how are you doing? I'm well, Shimon. How are you? I'm great. I'm excited to speak about Brooklyn because we see a lot happening there. And today we're going to touch on the six-month report that we've seen coming up from Ariel. The first six months of the year, about $3.5 billion of transactions, 15% higher than the last year, and it's substantial. Not everything did super well in terms of transactions. And I wanted to touch on two major aspects of this report. One is development, and two is multifamily. And specifically in the multifamily sector, I want to focus on one aspect. But let's start with development. We've seen a billion dollars worth of transactions in the first half of the year. That's a 60% increase year over year. And it's because of policy or some policy alignment. What do we see there? Sean, I know that you do a lot of development deals. What do we see there? What's really happening? Let's go with development. Sure. So, Shimon, we talk about this all the time. We've talked about this on the podcast before. you hit the nail on the head Is it policy Well it policy aligned with good incentives All right So we have a tax abatement that works for projects under 99 units So a lot of the transactional volume we've seen this year in the past six months came from a combination of the rezoning of the Atlantic Avenue corridor, right, in Crown Heights and Bedford-Stuyvesant, coupled with having the 485 tax abatement. We also saw, and this is not an anomaly, right? We've seen a flight to quality. So in terms of locations, there was a, you know, of the billion dollars in transactional volume, 300 million of it came from transactions in the greater downtown Brooklyn area. Well, let's take a step back again and let's talk about zoning initiatives and incentives. One of those large transactions was in the Navy Yard in Clinton Hill, a project that was slated five or six years ago, a little bit longer than that, to be an office conversion. And when post-COVID, the office market really, really struggled, the owners of that site went and had it rezoned. And that rezoning allowed them to sell it, probably get out of it whole, but it's going to create another 700 units in a really supply constrained market with a great job hub right there. Yeah. We then have, and then just in terms of flight to quality, we've seen improved pricing across all of the development sectors, right? So from the rental housing perspective, and frankly, we've seen increase in land prices because rents are higher because we not producing enough housing but we not producing enough housing in the free market sector So we seen increased land prices in pockets and project sizes where the execution will be to build condominiums or townhouses, and not surprisingly, a demand for affordable housing. And currently this year, I think in Brooklyn alone, we've sold $130 million in real estate. They were in contract for another $100 million, and it covers all of those food groups of the development market. That's pretty incredible. And you mentioned rents, and rents have grown a lot throughout the city, but specifically in prime locations in Brooklyn. And that helps the fundamentals of free market buildings. It doesn't help rent-stabilized housing. And what we see in rent-stabilized housing, which I found interesting, is the stress. We've seen the Pinnacle portfolio sale.
